title: A Partner Agreement Is a Plan for the Day You Disagree
summary: A partner agreement is not written for the good years. It is written for the day two partners stop agreeing, run short of money, or one of them can no longer take part. This lesson sets out the five clauses that decide who controls the asset on that day.
body:
A partner agreement earns its fee on the worst day of the partnership, not the first. Its job is to decide, in advance and in writing, what happens when partners disagree, run short of cash, want out, or can no longer act.

Recall

Q. In a joint venture, what is a reserved matter, sometimes called a major decision?

A. A decision the managing partner cannot make alone, such as selling the asset, refinancing, approving the budget or changing the business plan. It needs the consent of the other partner or a defined majority.

Q. When you negotiate with a lender, what can you usually trade?

A. Price against protection. You can trade a lower rate for more recourse, a higher loan for tighter covenants, or a faster close for fewer conditions. Decide your priorities before the term sheet arrives.

Q. What does the arm's length principle require in transfer pricing?

A. That related companies price their dealings as unrelated parties would in comparable circumstances, and keep the evidence that they did.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, most of the deals you will do in the next ten years will have a partner in them: a landowner, an investor, a co-developer, a contractor who takes equity instead of fee. Every one of those partnerships begins with goodwill. Many end with a dispute, and the dispute is rarely about character. It is about a question nobody answered in the document. Who decides when we disagree? What happens if one of us cannot fund? Can one of us sell and leave the other with a stranger? What happens if one of us dies?

A developer who answers those questions at signing keeps control of his project on the bad day. A developer who leaves them blank hands that control to a court, a lender, or the most stubborn partner in the room.

Vesting: equity is earned, not granted

In plain English: when one partner brings money and the other brings work, the working partner's share should be earned as the work is done, not handed over on day one.

The professional term is vesting: a share of ownership becomes permanent only as defined conditions are met, either over time or at milestones. A share that has not vested can be forfeited or bought back at a low price if the partner leaves. Development deals usually vest on milestones rather than months, because the work that creates value is lumpy: securing the land, winning the approvals, closing the loan, completing the building.

Worked example one, hypothetical round numbers. An investor puts in 4,000,000 dollars of cash. You bring the deal and your time, and the agreement gives you 30 percent of the profit above a return of capital. Without vesting, if you walk away in month three, you keep 30 percent of a project you did not build. With milestone vesting, you might earn a third of your share when the approvals are granted, a third at construction loan close, and the last third at completion. Leave after approvals, and you keep one third of your 30 percent, which is 10 percent. The investor is protected, and so are you, because a good vesting clause also says what happens if the investor blocks a milestone you could otherwise have reached.

Deadlock: the clause that ends an argument

In plain English: if two partners with equal votes cannot agree on something that matters, the business stops. A deadlock clause decides how it starts again.

Deadlock is the state where a required decision cannot be made because the partners who must consent will not agree. The usual ladder, which is commercial practice and not a legal standard, runs from escalation to the principals, to mediation, to an expert decision on technical questions, and finally to an exit mechanism. The most common exit is a buy-sell clause, often called a shotgun: one partner names a price for the whole equity, and the other must either buy at that price or sell at that price. Because the partner naming the price does not know which side he will end up on, he has a reason to name a fair one.

Worked example two, hypothetical. Two partners each hold 50 percent of a completed building. One wants to sell now; the other wants to hold for five years. Selling is a reserved matter, so nothing happens. Without a deadlock clause, they hold by default, and the partner who wanted out has his money trapped. With a buy-sell clause after a two-year lockout period, the selling partner names an equity value of 6,000,000 dollars. The holding partner must now either pay 3,000,000 dollars for the other half or accept 3,000,000 dollars for his own. The argument ends in a transaction, not a lawsuit.

Say that out loud now.

A deadlock clause turns an argument into a transaction.

Drag and tag, capital calls, and the three Ds

Drag-along and tag-along are paired rights on a sale. A drag-along lets a majority that agrees to sell to a third party force the minority to sell on the same terms, so a buyer can get the whole asset. A tag-along lets the minority join a sale by the majority on the same terms, so it is not left behind with a new partner it never chose. Each needs a floor: a minimum price, the same form of consideration, and no side payments to the majority.

Capital calls and dilution come next. A capital call is a demand for more equity under the agreement. The clause must say how much can be called, for what purposes, with what notice, and what happens to a partner who does not pay. Day 3 prices those remedies.

Finally, the three Ds: death, disability and divorce. Each can put a partner's interest in the hands of an estate, a guardian or a former spouse. The agreement should say whether the interest can transfer, whether the others have a right to buy it, how it is valued, and how the purchase is funded, often by insurance. A hypothetical estate that inherits half a construction project, with no money and no expertise, is a deadlock waiting to happen.

How the best do it

Large institutional joint ventures commonly treat the exit clauses as the core of the agreement rather than the end of it. They set a lockout period, then a buy-sell or forced-sale right, and they define the valuation method, the appraiser and the timetable before the first dollar moves. A small developer can copy the habit directly: draft the exit section first, and only then negotiate the economics.

Omar's Six-Lens Check

Tax. How a buyout is paid, as a purchase of an interest or a redemption by the entity, can change who is taxed and how; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability. Hold the asset in a limited-liability vehicle so a partner dispute stays inside it. Banking. Lenders often require consent to any change of control, so a buy-sell can trigger a loan default unless the loan allows it. Governance. Reserved matters and deadlock steps belong in the same document and must agree. Estate. The three D clauses decide what your heirs actually receive. Exit. Every partnership needs at least one route out that does not need the other partner's consent.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a 50-50 partnership with reserved matters and no deadlock exit. It works until the first serious disagreement, then freezes the asset. The control is a written deadlock ladder that ends in a mechanism one partner can trigger alone, such as a buy-sell or a forced sale, with a valuation method agreed at signing.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner negotiates the profit split for three weeks and accepts the default clauses in an afternoon, because talking about death, divorce and default feels like distrust. Experienced partners know the opposite: agreeing the hard clauses while everyone still likes each other is the only time it is easy.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema taught the pre-mortem: imagine the project has already failed and ask why. Run that drill on a partnership and the answers are almost always the five clauses in this lesson: a partner who stopped working, a deadlock, a sale nobody could force, a call nobody funded, or a partner who died. A partner agreement is a pre-mortem written as a contract.

Recap

Vesting makes contributed work earn its equity. A deadlock ladder ends in a mechanism one partner can trigger. Drag and tag decide who can force or join a sale. Capital call clauses must say what happens to the partner who does not pay. The three D clauses decide who holds an interest after death, disability or divorce. Professional sign-off required: lawyer, for the partner agreement.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: a composite partnership that froze when the money ran short.
checklist: Does my share vest on milestones I control, and what happens if my partner blocks one?
Is there a deadlock ladder that ends in a mechanism one partner can trigger alone?
Is the valuation method for any buy-sell agreed now, with the appraiser and timetable?
Do drag and tag rights carry a minimum price and identical terms for everyone?
Does the capital call clause state amount, purpose, notice and the remedy for non-payment?
What happens to each partner's interest on death, disability or divorce, and how is the purchase funded?
Will the lender's change-of-control clause allow the exit mechanisms to work?
head: Field checklist
speak: A partner agreement is written for the worst day of the partnership. Five clauses do the work. Vesting means a partner who contributes work earns his equity at milestones, so a partner who leaves early keeps only what he earned. A deadlock clause turns an argument into a transaction: escalation, mediation, then a mechanism one partner can trigger alone, usually a buy-sell where one names a price and the other must buy or sell at it. Drag and tag decide who can force or join a sale, and both need a price floor and identical terms. A capital call clause must say how much, for what, with what notice, and what happens to a partner who does not pay. And the three Ds, death, disability and divorce, decide who holds an interest when a partner can no longer act. Agree the exit section first, while everyone still trusts each other.
terms: Vesting — the process by which an ownership share becomes permanent only as defined time or milestone conditions are met.
Deadlock — the state where a required decision cannot be made because the partners who must consent will not agree.
Drag-along and tag-along — paired sale rights: the majority can force the minority to sell on the same terms, and the minority can join a majority sale on the same terms.

hostile.q: You want 30 percent of the profit for bringing the deal. What happens to that 30 percent if you stop working on it after six months?
hostile.a: It vests on milestones, so I only keep what I have earned. A third vests at approvals, a third at construction loan close and a third at completion. If I leave before approvals I keep nothing of the promote; if I leave after, I keep one third. If you block a milestone I could otherwise have reached, the agreement treats it as reached. That protects your capital from a partner who walks away, and protects my work from a partner who stalls.

title: The 50-50 Partnership That Froze When the Money Ran Short
summary: This is a composite example of two equal partners who built a clean deal on a handshake-level agreement with no deadlock exit and a vague capital call clause. When costs rose and one partner could not fund, the asset froze, the lender stepped in and both lost. Cole assists on the legal reading.
body:
This is a composite example. Two equal partners signed an agreement that described the deal well and the disagreement not at all. When a capital call went unanswered, nothing in the document could force a decision, and the lender made it for them.

Recall

Q. Who usually holds the drafting pen on a joint venture agreement, and why does it matter?

A. Commonly the managing partner or the larger investor. The first draft sets the frame for every later concession, so whoever drafts controls the defaults.

Q. What is a debt service coverage ratio covenant?

A. A promise in the loan that net operating income will stay at or above a stated multiple of debt service. A breach can trigger cash sweeps, reserves or a default. The ratio is a commercial term.

Q. What is a value-added tax?

A. A tax charged at each stage of supply on the value added, where registered businesses usually recover the tax they pay on inputs against the tax they charge on outputs.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me today because this failure was legal before it was financial. Nobody stole anything. Nobody built badly. Two capable people signed a document that did not contain the answers they would need, and when they needed them, there was no one with the authority to decide. The numbers are hypothetical round figures.

1. Timeline

Year 0: two developers form a company, 50 percent each, to build a 40-unit rental building. Total cost 20,000,000 dollars, funded by a 14,000,000 dollar construction loan and 6,000,000 dollars of equity, 3,000,000 dollars from each partner. The agreement names both as directors, makes every budget change a unanimous decision, and says that "further capital shall be contributed as required in proportion to shareholdings." Month 14: a structural redesign and a rate rise push cost to complete 2,000,000 dollars over budget. The lender declares the loan out of balance and requires a deposit. Partner A can fund 1,000,000 dollars. Partner B cannot fund anything. Month 15: Partner A proposes a call; Partner B votes against it. Month 17: with no deposit, the lender stops draws. Month 20: the contractor stops work. Month 24: the lender enforces and sells the unfinished building at a discount that wipes out all equity.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions shaped the result. Choosing equal shares with unanimous consent on every material decision. Accepting a capital call clause that said capital was "required" without saying who decides it is required, by when it must be paid, or what happens if it is not. And, in month 15, Partner A choosing to argue for three months rather than paying the deposit himself and documenting a claim.

3. Assumptions

Both partners assumed they would always agree because they always had. They assumed "as required" meant both would pay. Partner B assumed that voting against the call protected him, when it only stopped the project. Partner A assumed a court would quickly order B to pay. Cole's reading is different: a clause that does not say who decides, or what the remedy is, gives a court little to enforce, and litigation takes longer than a construction loan will wait.

4. Incentives

Partner B's incentive was to avoid putting more money into a project he could not afford, and to hope the problem solved itself. Partner A's incentive was not to fund B's share, because without a dilution or loan remedy, every dollar A paid in would be shared with B. The lender's incentive was to protect its loan, and once the loan was out of balance, its quickest protection was enforcement. Each choice was rational from where each party stood. None of them protected the equity.

Say that out loud now.

A clause that does not name the remedy has no remedy.

5. Warning signs ignored

The drafting lawyer's note at signing, suggesting a deadlock clause, was declined as "unnecessary between friends." Partner B had borrowed his original 3,000,000 dollars, which meant he had no reserve for a second call. The structural redesign was flagged in month 9, five months before the overrun was formally measured. And the lender's month-12 report noted that contingency was nearly exhausted. Any one of these was enough to start the conversation about who would fund an overrun.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was month 17, when draws stopped. Before that, Partner A could have deposited the full 2,000,000 dollars, or found a third investor to buy into B's half, or agreed a sale of B's interest at a discount. After draws stopped, the contractor's clock started, and a half-finished building loses value every week it stands still.

7. Root cause

The root cause was not the overrun. Overruns happen. The root cause was a partnership agreement with no deadlock exit and no capital call remedy. When the partners disagreed, the document could not break the tie, and when one could not pay, the document could not make the other's payment worth making.

Cole's reading: what the clause should have said

Cole's version of the capital call clause has five parts. Who may issue a call: the managing partner, for defined purposes such as an out-of-balance deposit or an emergency. How much: up to a cap, or more with consent. Notice: a fixed period, perhaps ten business days. Remedy: if one partner does not pay, the other may fund the shortfall either as a partner loan at a stated premium rate, repaid first from cash flow, or as additional equity that dilutes the defaulting partner. And a link to deadlock: a partner in default loses its vote on reserved matters until it cures. None of these numbers is a standard. All of them are negotiable. What matters is that each is written down.

What Partner A could still have done

Ford's reconstruction of month 15 is worth rehearsing, because it is the moment most developers will actually face. Partner A had 1,000,000 dollars of his own and needed 2,000,000 dollars. He had three moves open. He could have borrowed the second 1,000,000 dollars personally and deposited the full amount, accepting a weak claim against B, on the reasoning that a finished building with a messy claim is worth far more than an unfinished one with a clean grievance. He could have offered B's half to a third investor at a discount, with B's written consent obtained while B still had something to sell. Or he could have proposed an amendment to the agreement, adding a loan remedy, in exchange for B keeping his directorship. Each option cost something. Each was cheaper than enforcement.

The general lesson is that once a project is in trouble, the best remedy is the one you can execute inside the lender's timetable, not the one you are entitled to in theory. A clause written in advance gives you that remedy without a negotiation. Without it, you are negotiating against the clock and against a partner who has nothing left to lose.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an equal partnership where any one partner can block the decision that keeps the loan in balance. The control is a capital call clause with a named decision-maker, a notice period and a remedy, plus a deadlock ladder that ends in a buy-sell or forced sale.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes a vote against a call protects his money. It protects nothing. If the project needs the money and does not get it, every partner's equity is at risk, including his.

Callback

In Week 40, Priya taught the in-balance test: undisbursed loan plus remaining equity must cover cost to complete, or the borrower deposits the gap. This partnership failed that test and then discovered it had no way to decide who would make the deposit. The lender's test was clear. The partners' agreement was not.

Recap

Two equal partners, unanimous consent, a vague capital call, an overrun, one partner who could not fund, and no way to break the tie. The lender broke it by enforcing. The prevention is a funding remedy and a deadlock exit written before the money goes in.

Rule 69: Never sign a partnership without a capital call clause that names who calls, the notice period and the remedy for a partner who does not pay, and a deadlock ladder that ends in a buy-sell or forced sale one partner can trigger alone.

Next: JAX on The Money: what dilution and partner loans do to each partner's share and return.
checklist: Who has authority to issue a capital call, and for what defined purposes?
What is the cap on calls without further consent?
What is the notice period, and is it shorter than the lender's cure period?
What is the remedy if a partner does not fund: partner loan, dilution, or both?
Does a defaulting partner lose its vote until it cures?
Can each partner show a reserve for at least one capital call?
Does the deadlock ladder end in a mechanism one partner can trigger alone?
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite example. Two partners held 50 percent each, with unanimous consent on every material decision and a capital call clause that said only that capital would be contributed as required. An overrun put the loan out of balance. One partner could fund half, the other nothing. The second voted against the call, the first would not fund alone because every dollar he paid would be shared, and the lender stopped draws and enforced. The equity was wiped out. The overrun was not the root cause; overruns happen. The root cause was an agreement with no named decision-maker for calls, no remedy for non-payment, and no deadlock exit. Rule 69: never sign a partnership without a capital call clause that names who calls, the notice and the remedy, and a deadlock ladder that ends in a buy-sell or forced sale one partner can trigger alone.
terms: Capital call — a demand, made under the partnership agreement, for partners to contribute more equity.
Partner loan remedy — a clause letting a funding partner cover a defaulting partner's share as a loan at a stated rate, repaid ahead of distributions.
Point of no return — the last moment at which a decision could still have changed the outcome.

hostile.q: Your partner agreement says capital will be contributed as required. If your partner refuses, how does the money arrive before my next draw?
hostile.a: As written, it does not arrive reliably, so we are amending the agreement before closing. The managing partner may call for out-of-balance deposits on ten business days' notice. If a partner does not fund, the other may fund the shortfall as a partner loan at a premium rate repaid first, or as dilutive equity, and the defaulting partner loses its vote until it cures. Each partner is also holding a reserve for one call, which I can evidence.

rule: Rule 69: Never sign a partnership without a capital call clause that names who calls, the notice period and the remedy for a partner who does not pay, and a deadlock ladder that ends in a buy-sell or forced sale one partner can trigger alone.

title: What Dilution and Partner Loans Do to Your Share
summary: When a partner does not answer a capital call, the remedy decides who owns what afterwards. This lesson prices three remedies, plain dilution, penalty dilution and a partner loan, and shows how each moves ownership and return. Warrick's Wealth Ledger closes it.
body:
The remedy for an unpaid capital call is not a legal detail. It is a price, and it moves ownership, cash flow and return between partners. Know the price before you sign.

Recall

Q. In a joint venture, why are reporting obligations part of governance?

A. Because a partner cannot exercise its consent rights without timely, accurate information. Reporting is how control is exercised by the partner who is not on site.

Q. What is a debt yield, and why do lenders like it?

A. Net operating income divided by the loan amount. Lenders like it because it does not depend on the interest rate or the amortisation, only on how much income supports each dollar lent.

Q. What is input tax credit recovery under a value-added tax?

A. The process by which a registered business recovers the tax it paid on its purchases against the tax it charges on its sales. Rules and eligibility vary; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, on Day 2 the agreement had no remedy, and the project died. Today assumes the agreement has one. The question becomes: which remedy, and how harsh? Too soft, and the funding partner has no reason to fund. Too harsh, and a partner who misses one call by a week loses half his position, which a court may refuse to enforce, as LEX explains tomorrow. Every remedy below is commercial practice, negotiated deal by deal, and none is a standard.

Remedy one: plain dilution

In plain English: the partner who pays more owns more, in proportion to the money each has put in.

Worked example one, hypothetical round numbers. Partners A and B each contributed 5,000,000 dollars, so each owns 50 percent of 10,000,000 dollars of capital. The managing partner calls 2,000,000 dollars. A pays the whole 2,000,000 dollars because B cannot pay anything. Total capital is now 12,000,000 dollars. A has 7,000,000 dollars in, which is 7 divided by 12, or 58.3 percent. B has 5,000,000 dollars in, which is 41.7 percent.

Plain dilution is fair on its face, but it can be unfair to the funding partner. A took the risk of putting new money into a project in trouble, at a moment when the project's value may be below its cost. Plain dilution prices that new money at the original cost of the old money. It gives A nothing extra for rescuing the deal, and gives B no reason to find the money.

Remedy two: penalty dilution

Penalty dilution credits the funding partner with more than it paid for the purpose of calculating ownership. A common form multiplies the shortfall funded by a factor, such as 1.5, though the factor is entirely negotiated.

Same example. A funds B's 1,000,000 dollar share as well as its own 1,000,000 dollars. A's own 1,000,000 dollars counts at face value; the 1,000,000 dollars it funded for B counts at 1.5 times, or 1,500,000 dollars. A is credited with 5,000,000 plus 1,000,000 plus 1,500,000, which is 7,500,000 dollars. B stays at 5,000,000 dollars. Total credited capital is 12,500,000 dollars. A now owns 7.5 divided by 12.5, which is 60 percent, and B owns 40 percent.

The 1.7-point difference between 58.3 and 60 percent looks small. Now suppose the building eventually sells and leaves 20,000,000 dollars of equity value after the loan. Under plain dilution B receives 41.7 percent, about 8,340,000 dollars. Under penalty dilution B receives 40 percent, 8,000,000 dollars. The penalty cost B about 340,000 dollars for missing one call.

Say that out loud now.

The remedy is a price, paid at exit by the partner who missed the call.

Remedy three: the partner loan

A partner loan lets the funding partner advance the defaulting partner's share as a loan, usually at a premium rate, repaid out of the first available cash flow before ordinary distributions. Ownership does not change, but the defaulting partner's cash flow is diverted until the loan is repaid with interest.

Worked example two, hypothetical. A lends B's 1,000,000 dollar share at 15 percent simple interest, a negotiated rate, not a standard. Two years later the building refinances and distributes 4,000,000 dollars. Before any split, A is repaid 1,000,000 dollars of principal and 300,000 dollars of interest, a total of 1,300,000 dollars. The remaining 2,700,000 dollars is split 50-50, giving each partner 1,350,000 dollars. A receives 2,650,000 dollars in total. B receives 1,350,000 dollars and keeps his 50 percent going forward.

For B, the loan can be the better remedy if the project performs: B keeps his full share of future value and pays a known price. For A, the loan is attractive only if the rate truly reflects the risk of lending into a troubled project and if repayment ranks first. Many agreements let the funding partner choose between a loan and dilution, which gives A an option and makes B's default more expensive.

What the remedy does to return

For A, the 1,000,000 dollars advanced for B earns either a larger ownership share or a premium coupon. A should compare those as two investments: what return does a 1.7-point increase in ownership produce on the projected exit, against 15 percent with priority? For B, each remedy has an implied cost of capital, and that cost can be compared against the cost of borrowing elsewhere, selling part of his interest, or bringing in a new partner before the deadline.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, a partnership interest is an asset with a hidden liability attached: the obligation to answer capital calls. If you cannot answer one, the remedy clause tells you exactly how much of the asset you will lose. Hold a liquidity reserve sized to at least one realistic call on each partnership you are in, or negotiate a cap on calls that matches your reserve. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

Decision journals

This month's thread is the decision journal. Before you sign a remedy clause, write one paragraph: which remedy you chose, what you expect it to cost you if you are the partner who misses a call, what it should earn you if you are the one who funds, and what would make you change your mind.

Read that entry the first time a call is issued. The journal does not tell you whether you were lucky. It tells you whether you understood the price you agreed to.

Choosing between them

Here is a practical way to choose. If the project's trouble is temporary and the value is intact, a partner loan suits both sides: the funder earns a fair premium, the defaulting partner keeps his upside, and ownership stays simple for the lender, which often prefers that control does not shift. If the trouble is structural and the value is uncertain, the funder is taking real equity risk, and dilution, perhaps with a modest factor, is the honest price. Many sponsors write both into the agreement and give the funding partner the election within a short window, so the choice can follow the facts of the day. Whatever you pick, write the formula as arithmetic in the agreement, with a worked example in a schedule, so nobody has to argue about what the words meant.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is agreeing a harsh remedy without testing it from both sides. The control is to model each remedy twice: once as the partner who funds and once as the partner who cannot, on the same exit value.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks of dilution as an ownership percentage. It is money, received or lost at exit. Always translate the percentage into dollars on a realistic exit value.

Callback

In Week 38, JAX and Elias taught waterfalls: preferred return, catch-up and promote. A partner loan sits ahead of that waterfall, and dilution changes the percentages inside it. Run every capital call remedy through the waterfall, not only through the ownership table.

Recap

Plain dilution rewards new money at old cost. Penalty dilution credits the funder with a multiple, which is a price paid at exit by the partner who missed. A partner loan keeps ownership but diverts cash flow at a premium rate. Model every remedy from both sides, in dollars.

Next: LEX on The Rules: how courts read partner agreements, penalties and the forced-sale clause.
checklist: Have I modelled each remedy as both the funding and the defaulting partner?
Have I translated each dilution percentage into dollars on a realistic exit value?
Is a partner loan repaid ahead of the waterfall, and at what rate?
Can the funding partner choose between a loan and dilution?
Does a penalty factor look like compensation for risk rather than punishment?
Do I hold a reserve sized to at least one realistic capital call?
Have I recorded the remedy and its expected cost in my decision journal?
head: Field checklist
speak: When a partner misses a capital call, the remedy is a price, paid at exit. Plain dilution recalculates ownership on money actually contributed, so new money is priced at the cost of the old money and the rescuer gets nothing extra. Penalty dilution credits the funding partner with a multiple of what it advanced, for example 1.5 times, so the defaulting partner loses more of the eventual equity value. A partner loan keeps ownership the same but repays the funding partner, with a premium rate, out of the first cash flow, ahead of the waterfall. Each remedy should be modelled twice, once as the partner who funds and once as the partner who cannot, and translated into dollars on a realistic exit value. Personally, every partnership interest carries a call obligation, so I hold a reserve sized to at least one realistic call, or negotiate a cap that matches it.
terms: Plain dilution — recalculating ownership in proportion to the capital each partner has actually contributed.
Penalty dilution — a dilution formula that credits the funding partner with more than it paid, reducing the defaulting partner's share further.
Premium rate — the elevated interest rate charged on a partner loan, set to reflect the risk of lending into a troubled project.

hostile.q: Your penalty dilution factor is 2. If your partner misses one call by a week, he loses a large part of his equity. Why would a court enforce that?
hostile.a: It might not, and I do not want to rely on it. A factor of 2 can look like punishment rather than compensation for risk. I would rather give the funding partner a choice: a partner loan at a premium rate repaid first, or dilution at a moderate factor tied to the risk taken, with a cure period before either applies. That is easier to defend and still gives the funding partner a real reason to rescue the project.

title: How Courts Read a Partner Agreement
summary: A partner agreement is a contract, but between partners and co-owners the law adds duties and remedies the document does not always mention. This lesson covers how courts read harsh default clauses, the forced-sale clause and the shareholder remedy for unfair treatment, and compares the conceptual approach in Canada and Guyana.
body:
A court reads a partner agreement first as a contract, but it reads it in a relationship. The law of penalties, the duties partners owe one another and the remedy for unfair treatment can all reach past the words you signed.

Recall

Q. What is plain dilution after a missed capital call?

A. Recalculating ownership in proportion to the capital each partner has actually contributed, so the partner who funds more owns more.

Q. What is a cash sweep in a loan?

A. A provision that diverts some or all surplus cash flow to pay down the loan, often triggered when a coverage covenant is breached. Its terms are commercial, not standard.

Q. What is a customs duty?

A. A tax charged on goods as they cross a border, usually based on their classification and value, collected at import.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the clauses JAX priced yesterday only work if a court will enforce them. A partner who loses half his position for missing one call has every incentive to argue the clause is unenforceable, and the argument can freeze the project while it runs. Knowing how courts read these clauses lets you draft terms that survive the challenge. This is conceptual teaching. How any court will rule depends on its law and the facts; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

The penalty doctrine

In plain English: in common law systems, a court may refuse to enforce a clause whose real purpose is to punish a party for breaking the contract, rather than to protect a legitimate interest.

The penalty doctrine is the common law rule that a clause triggered by breach, which imposes a consequence out of all proportion to any legitimate interest of the innocent party, may be unenforceable. The modern statement in English law came in Cavendish Square Holding v Makdessi, decided by the United Kingdom Supreme Court in 2015, which concerned a seller of shares who breached restrictive covenants and, under the contract, lost deferred payments and had to sell his remaining shares at a lower price. The court asked whether the clause protected a legitimate interest in a proportionate way, and upheld it. Other common law courts, including Canadian courts, have their own versions of the test, and they are not identical. Verify against the current law of your jurisdiction.

Worked example one, hypothetical. A capital call remedy credits the funding partner at 3 times what it advanced, with no cure period. A partner misses a call of 200,000 dollars by four days and loses 12 percentage points of a project worth millions. That outcome invites a penalty argument. A version with a ten-day cure period, a factor of 1.25 and a recital explaining the funder's risk is far easier to defend, because the consequence is tied to a legitimate interest: getting new money into a project in trouble.

The forced-sale clause

The shotgun clause, introduced on Day 1, is a contractual buy-sell: one partner names a price, the other must buy or sell at it. Courts generally enforce these clauses as written when the procedure is followed exactly. Disputes usually turn on procedure: whether notice was served correctly, whether the price was stated in the required form, whether the deadline was met, whether funding was in place. A shotgun can also be used aggressively by a partner who knows the other cannot raise the money to buy. That is why careful drafters add protections: a longer response period, a requirement that the triggering partner shows proof of funds, and, sometimes, a right to bring in a third-party buyer.

Say that out loud now.

A shotgun is enforced on its procedure, so every step must be written and followed exactly.

Unfair treatment and the shareholder remedy

Where partners hold their interests through a company, many common law jurisdictions give shareholders a statutory remedy when the company's affairs are conducted in a way that is oppressive, unfairly prejudicial, or that unfairly disregards their interests. This is often called the oppression remedy. Courts in these systems commonly ask what the shareholder could reasonably expect, judged by the relationship and the agreements, and can order wide relief, including that one shareholder buy the other out. The availability, scope and test differ by statute; verify against the current law of your jurisdiction.

Worked example two, hypothetical. A majority partner, who controls the board, pays a related construction company above-market fees, never issues reports and calls capital the minority cannot meet. Even if each step fits the words of the agreement, a court may see the pattern as unfair to the minority's reasonable expectations. The lesson for drafting is direct: put related-party dealings, reporting and capital call purposes into the agreement, so reasonable expectations are written, not argued.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

This is a conceptual comparison; verify against primary source before relying on any point. Canada's federal and provincial corporate statutes provide, in general terms, for shareholder agreements and for a statutory remedy against oppressive or unfairly prejudicial conduct, and Canadian corporate law recognises a form of agreement among all shareholders that can restrict the directors' powers. Courts apply contract law and the penalty doctrine to the agreement itself. Guyana's company law also derives from the Commonwealth common law tradition, with its own companies statute that, in general terms, addresses shareholder remedies; the specific provisions and how its courts apply them should be confirmed. [unverified — confirm independently] In both, the practical rule is the same: a well-drafted agreement, with clear default and exit procedures, is far more predictable than any statutory remedy.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, qualified in the jurisdiction of the entity and of the asset.

Duties between partners

Where the vehicle is a partnership rather than a company, many common law systems treat partners as owing each other duties of good faith, and in some settings duties similar to a trustee's, particularly around partnership property and opportunities. A partner who quietly buys the neighbouring site for himself, when the partnership was looking for exactly that land, may be accountable for the profit. Companies are different: directors owe their duties to the company, and shareholders, as such, generally do not owe each other fiduciary duties unless an agreement or relationship creates them. That difference is one reason the choice of vehicle in Week 35 matters. Verify against the current law of your jurisdiction.

The three Ds in law

Death, disability and divorce each bring an outsider's legal rights into the partnership. An executor administers a deceased partner's estate and must act for its beneficiaries, not for the project. A guardian or attorney for an incapacitated partner must act within the authority granted. A divorcing spouse may have a property claim that reaches the interest. A transfer restriction and a purchase right in the agreement, drafted with estate and family counsel, decide how those rights meet the partnership.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a harsh default clause that a court refuses to enforce, after the partners have relied on it for years. The control is proportionality: cure periods, moderate factors, stated reasons tied to the funding partner's real risk, and legal review in the governing jurisdiction.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks the harshest clause gives the most protection. The clause that protects you is the one a court will enforce quickly, without a trial about whether it is fair.

Callback

In Week 20, LEX taught that contracts are enforced through conditions, breach and remedies, and that the remedy clause is often where the real negotiation happens. Partner agreements are the same contract law with a relationship added, which is why the law adds duties and remedies on top of the words.

Recap

Courts read partner agreements as contracts but may refuse to enforce penalties out of proportion to a legitimate interest. Shotgun clauses are enforced on their procedure. Shareholders in a company may have a statutory remedy against unfair treatment. Draft proportionate remedies, exact procedures and written expectations.

Next: JAX on The Numbers: working through a buy-sell price and a dilution, step by step.
checklist: Does every default remedy include a cure period?
Is any penalty factor proportionate and tied to a stated, legitimate interest?
Is the shotgun procedure written step by step: notice, form of price, deadline, funding proof?
Does the shotgun give enough time for the responding partner to raise funds?
Are related-party dealings and reporting duties written into the agreement?
Which jurisdiction's law governs the agreement and the entity, and has a local lawyer reviewed it?
Have I avoided relying on a statutory remedy instead of clear drafting?
head: Field checklist
speak: A partner agreement is read as a contract, but courts add rules. The penalty doctrine lets a common law court refuse to enforce a breach clause whose consequence is out of all proportion to a legitimate interest; the UK Supreme Court restated the test in Makdessi in 2015, and other courts, including Canadian ones, have their own versions. So I use cure periods, moderate dilution factors and stated reasons tied to the funder's real risk. Shotgun buy-sell clauses are enforced on procedure, so notice, form, deadline and proof of funds must be exact. Where partners hold through a company, many statutes give shareholders a remedy against oppressive or unfairly prejudicial conduct, judged against reasonable expectations, so I write related-party rules and reporting into the agreement. Canada and Guyana both draw on common law, but the details must be confirmed with a local lawyer.
terms: Penalty doctrine — the common law rule that a breach clause imposing a consequence out of proportion to a legitimate interest may be unenforceable.
Shotgun clause — a buy-sell clause in which one partner names a price and the other must either buy or sell at that price.
Oppression remedy — a statutory remedy, in many common law jurisdictions, for shareholders treated in an oppressive or unfairly prejudicial way.

hostile.q: You triggered the shotgun knowing your partner could not fund a purchase in thirty days. Isn't that oppressive?
hostile.a: The clause was negotiated by both of us with counsel, and I followed its procedure exactly. But I would not rely on that alone. Our clause gives ninety days, requires the triggering partner to show proof of funds, and lets the responding partner bring in a third-party buyer. Those terms exist precisely so the mechanism tests price, not liquidity, and I am willing to show the valuation evidence behind the number I named.

title: Pricing a Buy-Sell After a Missed Capital Call
summary: A worked calculation, with hypothetical round numbers, that takes a partnership through a missed capital call, a partner loan, and then a shotgun buy-sell. Every step shows its units, and the result shows why the price you name in a shotgun must survive being on either side of it.
body:
A buy-sell price is not a guess at value. It is a number you must be willing to pay and willing to accept, after every loan, call and priority in the agreement has been applied. Work it through step by step.

Recall

Q. What does a partner loan remedy do?

A. It lets the funding partner cover a defaulting partner's share as a loan at a stated rate, repaid from the first available cash flow ahead of distributions, without changing ownership.

Q. What is a refinance risk in a lender negotiation?

A. The risk that, when the loan matures, the property cannot support a new loan large enough to repay the old one, because value, income or credit conditions have moved.

Q. What is a tax holiday or investment concession?

A. A reduction or exemption from a tax, granted for a period or a project, usually in exchange for meeting conditions. The terms and conditions are set by the granting law; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the most expensive mistake in a shotgun is naming a price you have not tested from the other side. If you name too low, your partner buys you out cheaply. If you name too high, he sells to you, and you must find the money. The only safe number is one that works for you on both sides, after every claim on the equity has been counted. All numbers below are hypothetical round figures.

Step 1: the starting position

A partnership owns a stabilised apartment building. Partners A and B each contributed 4,000,000 dollars, total 8,000,000 dollars, and each owns 50 percent. The building has a first mortgage of 12,000,000 dollars. In year 2, the managing partner issues a capital call of 1,000,000 dollars for a roof replacement. A pays its 500,000 dollars. B does not pay. The agreement gives A the choice of a partner loan at 12 percent simple interest or dilution. A chooses the loan and advances B's 500,000 dollars.

Step 2: the partner loan after two years

Interest is 500,000 dollars times 12 percent, which is 60,000 dollars per year. After two years the interest is 120,000 dollars. The loan balance owed by B to A, repaid from B's share before any distribution, is 500,000 plus 120,000, which is 620,000 dollars.

Step 3: the value of the equity

In year 4, A triggers the shotgun. A must name a price for the whole of the equity. To choose it, A estimates the building's value. Net operating income (NOI) is 1,400,000 dollars per year. Using a market capitalisation rate of 7 percent, value is 1,400,000 divided by 0.07, which is 20,000,000 dollars. Selling costs and the cost of repaying the mortgage early, if any, are estimated at 400,000 dollars. Net value after costs is 19,600,000 dollars. Less the mortgage of 12,000,000 dollars, the equity is worth 7,600,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

The equity is the building, less the costs of selling, less the debt.

Step 4: applying the agreement to the price

Suppose A names a price of 7,600,000 dollars for 100 percent of the equity. The agreement says any partner loan is settled first out of the selling partner's proceeds, or credited to the buying partner. Each half of the equity is 3,800,000 dollars.

Outcome one: B elects to sell. A pays B 3,800,000 dollars for B's half, less the 620,000 dollar loan B owes A. Cash paid to B is 3,180,000 dollars. A's net cash outlay is 3,180,000 dollars, and A now owns 100 percent.

Outcome two: B elects to buy. B must pay A 3,800,000 dollars for A's half, plus repay the 620,000 dollar loan. Cash paid to A is 4,420,000 dollars. B must find that money within the response period, usually by new equity or by refinancing.

Step 5: testing the price from both sides

A's test is whether it is content with either outcome. If A believes the true equity value is 7,600,000 dollars, both outcomes give A fair value: either 100 percent for 3,180,000 dollars of new cash, or 4,420,000 dollars of cash out. Now imagine A instead names 6,000,000 dollars, hoping B cannot fund a purchase. Each half is 3,000,000 dollars. If B sells, B receives 3,000,000 less 620,000, which is 2,380,000 dollars, and A has bought cheaply. But if B finds an investor and buys, A receives only 3,000,000 plus 620,000, which is 3,620,000 dollars, for a half that is really worth 3,800,000 dollars. A has lost 180,000 dollars, and, worse, lost the building. Naming low only works if the other side truly cannot fund, and a well-drafted clause, as LEX explained, gives them time to try.

Step 6: a quick sensitivity

The capitalisation rate drives the result. If the market rate is 7.5 percent rather than 7 percent, value is 1,400,000 divided by 0.075, which is about 18,670,000 dollars. Net of 400,000 dollars of costs and 12,000,000 dollars of debt, equity is about 6,270,000 dollars. A half-point move in the rate moved the equity by about 1,330,000 dollars, or 17 percent. That is why both partners should agree, at signing, on the valuation method and the appraiser who will settle a dispute.

Step 7: what if A had chosen dilution instead

Go back to Step 1 and let A choose plain dilution rather than the loan. Capital before the call was 8,000,000 dollars. A paid 1,000,000 dollars, its own share and B's. A now has 5,000,000 dollars in and B has 4,000,000 dollars, out of 9,000,000 dollars total. A owns 5 divided by 9, which is 55.6 percent, and B owns 44.4 percent.

At the shotgun, equity of 7,600,000 dollars splits as 55.6 percent to A, about 4,222,000 dollars, and 44.4 percent to B, about 3,378,000 dollars. Compare with the loan route: there, B's half of 3,800,000 dollars less the 620,000 dollar loan gave B 3,180,000 dollars. So in this example, plain dilution leaves B about 198,000 dollars better off than the loan, because the building's value rose and B's diluted share still carried part of that rise, while the loan charged a fixed 12 percent regardless.

The answer would reverse if the value had fallen. That is the insight: a loan gives the funder a fixed return and leaves the upside and downside with the owners; dilution gives the funder a larger share of whatever happens. Which remedy is better for you depends on which side of the call you are on and what you expect the building to do. Run both before you elect.

One more check belongs in every version of this calculation: the lender. Many loan agreements treat a material change in ownership as needing consent, so a dilution that moves control, or a shotgun that leaves one partner owning everything, may need the lender's approval before it closes. Read the change-of-control clause before you trigger anything.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is naming a shotgun price that ignores the partner loan, selling costs or the debt, or one that only works if you end up on one side. The control is a written calculation, from NOI to net equity, through every priority in the agreement, tested in both outcomes.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner names a price for the building. The shotgun prices the equity, and the equity is what remains after costs, debt and partner claims. Confusing the two can move the answer by millions.

Callback

In Week 10, Sage taught that value is net operating income divided by a capitalisation rate, and that small moves in the rate make large moves in value. Here that arithmetic becomes a negotiation: the half-point you ignore is the money your partner keeps.

Recap

Settle the partner loan with interest, value the building from NOI and a capitalisation rate, deduct selling costs and debt to reach equity, apply the agreement's priorities, and test the price in both outcomes. Name only a number you will accept on either side.

Next: JAX on The Room: the meeting where your partner says he cannot fund the call.
checklist: Have I calculated any partner loan balance with interest to the shotgun date?
Have I valued the building from NOI and a capitalisation rate I can defend?
Have I deducted selling costs, prepayment costs and the mortgage to reach equity?
Have I applied every priority in the agreement to each partner's share?
Have I tested my price as both buyer and seller?
Have I run a sensitivity on the capitalisation rate?
Can I fund the purchase if my partner chooses to sell?
head: Field checklist
speak: Here is the calculation, hypothetical. Two partners hold 50 percent each. One missed a 500,000 dollar call, the other lent it at 12 percent, so after two years the loan balance is 620,000 dollars. The building earns 1,400,000 dollars of NOI. At a 7 percent capitalisation rate it is worth 20,000,000 dollars, less 400,000 dollars of selling costs and 12,000,000 dollars of debt, so the equity is 7,600,000 dollars, 3,800,000 dollars per half. If the indebted partner sells, he receives 3,800,000 less the 620,000 loan, 3,180,000 dollars. If he buys, he pays 3,800,000 plus 620,000, 4,420,000 dollars. A low price only works if he cannot fund; if he can, the low bidder loses value and the building. A half-point move in the rate moved the equity by about 17 percent. Name only a price I will accept on either side.
terms: Equity value — the value of the property after deducting selling costs, debt and any other claims ranking ahead of the partners.
Capitalisation rate — the ratio of net operating income to value used to convert income into a price.
Response period — the time a partner has, under a buy-sell clause, to elect to buy or sell and to fund the purchase.

hostile.q: You named a price of 7,600,000 dollars for the equity. Show me how you got there and why your partner loan is deducted from my share.
hostile.a: The building's NOI of 1,400,000 dollars at a 7 percent capitalisation rate gives 20,000,000 dollars. I deducted 400,000 dollars of estimated selling costs and the 12,000,000 dollar mortgage, which leaves 7,600,000 dollars of equity. The agreement says partner loans are settled out of the selling partner's proceeds, so the 620,000 dollars you owe, principal plus two years at 12 percent, comes off your half. If you dispute the capitalisation rate, the agreement names the appraiser who settles it.

title: The Meeting Where Your Partner Cannot Fund the Call
summary: A realistic scene: your partner tells you he cannot meet a capital call the lender needs within ten days. The lesson gives the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind his words, when to stay silent and how to keep your state steady while the clock runs.
body:
When a partner says he cannot fund, the meeting is not about blame. It is about which remedy runs, how fast, and whether the relationship survives it. Keep the clock, the clause and your composure in front of you.

Recall

Q. In a shotgun, what is the equity value you name?

A. The property's value less selling costs, debt and any claims ranking ahead of the partners, not the building's gross value.

Q. When should you walk away from a lender?

A. When the terms take more risk than the deal can carry, for example recourse or covenants you cannot meet in the downside case, and your alternative is better than the deal on offer. Know your alternative before you negotiate.

Q. What is a capital control?

A. A government measure that restricts the movement of money into or out of a country, such as limits on converting or sending currency abroad.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this conversation will happen to you. A partner you like, who has been reliable, calls and asks to meet. The lender wants a deposit in ten business days. His share is 500,000 dollars. He does not have it. How you handle the next hour decides whether the project is funded, whether the remedy is used fairly, and whether you keep a partner or make an enemy. The scene uses hypothetical figures.

The scene

A quiet room, not a restaurant. Your partner arrives with no papers. He says: "I'll be straight with you. I can't do the call. Money's tied up. I need some time. Can we just tell the bank to wait?"

Your first job is to hear the facts before you respond. Ask: "Thank you for telling me early. How much can you fund, by when, and is there anything that would change that?" Then stop talking. The silence after that question is where the real answer arrives. He may say he can fund 200,000 dollars in thirty days, or that his money is in another deal, or that his spouse has said no.

Say that out loud now.

How much can you fund, by when, and what would change that?

The question behind the question

When he asks the bank to wait, he is really asking: "Will this cost me my share, and will you use the clause against me?" Answer that directly, because if you do not, he will fill the gap with fear. "The bank will not wait; the deposit is due on the tenth. Here is what the agreement gives us. I can fund your share as a partner loan, at the rate in the agreement, repaid before distributions, and you keep your full ownership. Or the agreement allows dilution. I would rather do the loan, because it keeps us equal partners and gives you a way back."

The lines to say

Say what the document says, not what you feel about it. "Under section nine, the call is valid and the remedy is my choice." Offer the gentler remedy first if the economics work for you, and say why. Put the decision in writing the same day: "I'll send you a note tonight confirming what we agreed, so neither of us has to remember it." Name the next step and the date: "I'll fund on the eighth, and you'll have the loan statement on the ninth."

The lines never to say

Never say "Don't worry about it," because it sounds like a waiver of the remedy, and a court may later read it that way. Never say "I'll just take your share then," because it sounds like the punishment LEX warned against. Never make a side promise, such as forgiving the interest, that the agreement does not record. Never discuss his personal finances with the lender without his permission.

When to stay silent

Stay silent after you state the remedy. He needs time to understand that the clause is real and that you are not angry. Stay silent if he becomes emotional; do not argue with distress. And stay silent rather than agree to anything in the room that you have not checked against the agreement and the loan.

Holding your state

You will feel two pulls: sympathy, which tempts you to promise too much, and irritation, which tempts you to punish. Both distort the decision. Before the meeting, write on one card the deposit date, the amount, the two remedies and the one you prefer. Look at it when you feel the pull. If you need a reset, ask for five minutes and step outside, and while parked or seated, take a few slow breaths with a longer exhale. Check that with your doctor if you have any condition that breathing exercises might affect.

How the best do it

Experienced sponsors separate the person from the mechanism. They issue every capital call in the same written form, apply the remedy exactly as written, and keep a call register showing the date of each notice, each payment and each election. A small developer can copy that discipline from the first deal: a template call notice, a register and a same-day written confirmation of every conversation about money.

The second half of the meeting

Once the remedy is understood, move the conversation to what comes next, because a partner who could not fund once may not fund the next call either. Ask, calmly: "If there is another call in the next twelve months, what would you be able to do?" If the honest answer is nothing, raise the options while the relationship is still warm: bringing in a third investor to take part of his interest, a planned sale of part of his share to you at a value set by the agreed method, or a cap on future calls with a matching contingency held at the project level. Do not decide them in the room. Agree to put them on paper and meet again within a week.

If he becomes angry

Anger in this meeting is usually fear of loss. Do not match it, and do not defend yourself. Acknowledge it once: "I understand this is hard, and I would feel the same." Then return to the facts: the date, the amount, the remedy. If the anger continues, end the meeting politely and propose a time to resume, perhaps with each of your lawyers present. A conversation that becomes a fight produces nothing you can rely on, and the deposit date does not move.

Afterwards, write down what was said while it is fresh, with the time and the people present. That note, made the same day, is worth far more than a memory reconstructed months later in a dispute.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an informal promise in the room that undercuts the written remedy, so neither the loan nor the dilution can later be enforced cleanly. The control is to say only what the agreement says, and confirm every agreement in writing the same day.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner tries to protect the friendship by being vague. Vagueness is what turns a funding problem into a dispute. Clear terms, kindly stated, protect the friendship better.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught "acknowledge, bridge, answer" for hostile questions, and the discipline of "I'll confirm by Friday." Here the same pattern runs in reverse: acknowledge that he told you early, bridge to what the agreement says, answer with the remedy and the date, then confirm in writing tonight.

Recap

Get the facts first, then answer the fear behind the question. State the remedy the agreement gives, offer the gentler one if it works, confirm in writing the same day, and never make a side promise. Hold your state with a card and, if needed, a short break.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: Week 69's six questions, the Red Pen and the boardroom drill.
checklist: Have I written the deposit date, amount and both remedies on one card before the meeting?
Did I ask how much, by when, and what would change it, then stay silent?
Did I answer the fear behind his request directly?
Did I state the remedy the agreement gives, by section?
Did I avoid any side promise not in the agreement?
Did I send a same-day written confirmation with the next step and date?
Have I updated the capital call register?
head: Field checklist
speak: When a partner says he cannot fund a call, I get the facts first: how much can you fund, by when, and what would change that, then I stay silent. His real question is whether this will cost him his share and whether I will use the clause against him, so I answer that directly. The bank will not wait; the deposit is due on the tenth. The agreement lets me fund his share as a partner loan at the agreed rate, repaid first, and he keeps his ownership, or it allows dilution. I prefer the loan and say why. I never say don't worry, never threaten to take his share, never make a side promise, and never discuss his finances with the lender without his permission. I confirm in writing the same day, and keep a register of every call, payment and election.
terms: Call register — a written record of each capital call notice, payment and remedy election, with dates.
Waiver — giving up a contractual right, which can happen by words or conduct as well as in writing.
Election — a choice a party is entitled to make under a contract, such as which remedy to apply.

hostile.q: Last month you told me not to worry about the call. Now you are charging me 12 percent. Haven't you waived the remedy?
hostile.a: I understand why you read it that way, and I should have been more precise. What I meant was that we would find a solution. The agreement says waivers must be in writing, and my email the same evening set out the partner loan at the agreed rate. I am applying exactly what that email and section nine say, and I am offering the loan rather than dilution so you keep your full share.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 69 Review: Vesting, Deadlock, Calls and the Three Ds
summary: Six questions test the week's core ideas: vesting, deadlock, drag and tag, capital call remedies, penalties and the shotgun. The Red Pen drill marks up a hypothetical partner agreement clause, and a two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: a partner agreement must decide, before the money goes in, who controls the asset when partners disagree, cannot pay, want out or can no longer act.

Recall

Q. What is a reserved matter in a joint venture?

A. A decision that needs the consent of a partner other than the manager, such as a sale, refinancing or budget approval.

Q. What should you ask a lender for if you value certainty of close over price?

A. Fewer and clearer conditions precedent, a committed timetable and an agreed form of closing documents, accepting that you may pay for them in rate or fees.

Q. Why does transfer pricing documentation matter?

A. Because a tax authority can adjust related-party prices it believes are not at arm's length, and documentation prepared at the time is the main defence.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will sign partner agreements under time pressure, usually with the land deadline close. If you can answer these six questions aloud without notes, you can read the clauses that matter in an hour and know which ones to fight for. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Why should contributed work vest on milestones rather than be granted on day one?

Answer: Because a partner who leaves early would otherwise keep a share of value he did not create. Milestone vesting ties equity to the steps that create value, such as approvals, loan close and completion, and should treat a milestone as reached if the other partner blocks it.

Question 2. What should a deadlock ladder end with?

Answer: A mechanism one partner can trigger alone, such as a buy-sell or a forced sale, with the valuation method agreed in advance. Escalation and mediation come first, but without a final step the asset can freeze.

Question 3. What protections should a drag-along carry?

Answer: A minimum price, the same terms and form of consideration for all sellers, and no side payments to the majority.

Question 4. Name three remedies for a missed capital call and their economic effect.

Answer: Plain dilution, which reprices ownership on capital actually paid. Penalty dilution, which credits the funder with a multiple and costs the defaulter more at exit. A partner loan at a premium rate, repaid first, which keeps ownership but diverts cash flow.

Question 5. When might a court refuse to enforce a harsh default clause?

Answer: When, under the penalty doctrine in a common law system, the consequence is out of all proportion to any legitimate interest of the innocent party. Cure periods, moderate factors and stated reasons make a clause easier to defend.

Question 6. Why must a shotgun price be tested from both sides?

Answer: Because the partner naming the price does not choose whether he buys or sells. A low price works only if the other side cannot fund, and a well-drafted clause gives it time to try.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

JAX framed the five clauses that decide control on the bad day. Ford and Cole took a composite 50-50 partnership that froze when one partner could not fund, giving Rule 69. JAX priced plain dilution, penalty dilution and the partner loan. LEX showed how courts read penalties, shotguns and unfair treatment, and compared Canada and Guyana. JAX worked a buy-sell price through a partner loan. JAX ran the meeting with a partner who could not fund.

The Red Pen

Read this hypothetical clause and find the defects before reading on.

Section 9. Further Capital. The Partners shall contribute such further capital as may be required from time to time. If a Partner fails to contribute, the other Partner may contribute on its behalf and the defaulting Partner's interest shall be reduced accordingly by a factor of 3. Disputes shall be resolved by the Partners negotiating in good faith. On the death of a Partner, the surviving Partner may purchase the deceased Partner's interest at fair value. Either Partner may require the other to join any sale of the Property.

The defects. First, "as may be required" does not say who decides that capital is required, for what purposes, or up to what amount. Second, there is no notice period and no cure period. Third, "reduced accordingly by a factor of 3" is ambiguous about the formula, and a factor of 3 with no cure invites a penalty challenge. Fourth, there is no partner loan alternative and no loss of voting rights while in default. Fifth, "negotiating in good faith" is not a deadlock mechanism; there is no exit one partner can trigger. Sixth, "fair value" on death is undefined, with no valuation method, appraiser or timetable, and no funding source such as insurance. Seventh, the drag-along in the last sentence lets either partner force the other into any sale, with no minimum price and no requirement of identical terms. And disability and divorce are missing entirely.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to an investor who asks, "What happens if you and your partner fall out?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "We decided that before we signed. My share vests on milestones, so if I stop working, I keep only what I earned. Major decisions need both of us, but if we deadlock we escalate, mediate, and then either of us can trigger a buy-sell after a lockout, at a value set by an agreed method and appraiser. If one of us cannot fund a capital call, the other can lend the money at an agreed rate, repaid first, or take dilution, after a cure period, and the defaulting partner loses its vote until it cures. Drag and tag rights carry a minimum price and identical terms. On death, disability or divorce, the others can buy the interest at an agreed valuation, funded by insurance. So a falling-out ends in a transaction, not a frozen building."

Score yourself: bottom line first? Deadlock exit named? Capital call remedy with a cure period? Three Ds covered? Inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

How the clause should read

Here is the shape of a better Section 9, in outline. The Managing Partner may call further capital, on ten business days' written notice, for defined purposes: an out-of-balance deposit, an emergency repair, or an approved budget item, up to a stated cap without further consent. If a Partner does not fund by the due date and does not cure within five further business days, the funding Partner may elect, within ten business days, either a partner loan at a stated rate, repaid ahead of all distributions, or dilution using a formula set out in a schedule with a worked example, at a moderate factor. While in default, a Partner has no vote on reserved matters. Deadlock goes to escalation, mediation, and then, after a lockout period, a buy-sell with a defined procedure. On death, disability or divorce, the others may purchase at a value fixed by a named appraisal method, funded in part by insurance. A drag-along requires a minimum price and identical terms for all sellers.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is signing a partner agreement whose default and exit clauses were accepted as boilerplate. The control is to read and negotiate the exit section first, and to model every remedy in dollars.

The beginner's mistake

Treating a friendly relationship as a substitute for clear terms. The terms protect the friendship when money runs short.

Callback

In Week 33, JAX and Omar taught landowner joint ventures and valuing contributed land. Every one of those deals needs this week's clauses: a landowner who contributes land and then cannot fund a call is the most common deadlock in development.

Recap

Vesting, deadlock, drag and tag, capital calls and the three Ds decide control on the bad day. Remedies are prices, courts test proportionality, and shotgun prices must work from both sides. Rule 69 makes the call and the exit explicit.

head: The six questions
speak: A partner agreement decides control on the bad day. Contributed work vests on milestones, so a partner who leaves keeps only what he earned. Deadlock goes to escalation, mediation, then a buy-sell or forced sale either partner can trigger, at an agreed valuation method. Drag and tag rights carry a minimum price and identical terms. A missed capital call triggers a remedy after a cure period: plain dilution, penalty dilution, or a partner loan at a premium rate repaid first, and each is a price I model in dollars from both sides. Courts may refuse penalties out of proportion to a legitimate interest, and enforce shotguns on their procedure. The three Ds, death, disability and divorce, need a buyout right, a valuation and a funding source. Rule 69: name who calls, the notice and the remedy, and end the deadlock ladder in a mechanism one partner can trigger alone.
terms: Cure period — the time a party has, after notice, to remedy a default before the remedy applies.
Lockout period — an initial period during which a buy-sell or forced sale cannot be triggered.
Three Ds — death, disability and divorce, the events that can move a partner's interest to someone else.

hostile.q: Your agreement lets you dilute me by a factor of 3 if I miss a call. Why should I sign that?
hostile.a: You should not, and I have withdrawn it. The revised clause gives ten business days' notice and a cure period, then lets the funding partner choose a partner loan at an agreed rate repaid first, or dilution at a moderate factor tied to the risk of funding a troubled project. A defaulting partner loses its vote until it cures. That is fair to whichever of us ends up funding, and it is far more likely to be enforced.
